entry.title: Implementing IFRS S1 and S2 Sustainability Disclosure Standards with End‑to‑End Reporting Flows
entry.content:
This article reflects the collective efforts of several contributors: Bilge Akdur, Elsa Sandoval Ruiz, Julia Sabrowski

Introduction

The IFRS® Sustainability Disclosure Standards, IFRS S1 (General Requirements for Disclosure of Sustainability-Related Financial Information) and IFRS S2 (Climate-Related Disclosures), issued in June 2023 and effective for annual reporting periods beginning on or after 1 January 2024, are a common baseline for sustainability-related financial disclosure. As a growing number of jurisdictions around the world are adopting these standards, organizations are increasingly expected to report on climate-related risks and opportunities comparable to those applied in financial reporting. Sustainability reporting is dynamic by design as it considers material impacts, risks, and opportunities. Investors, for example, can now look to sustainability KPIs as signals to move from mostly stewardship non-financial reporting to financial-grade sustainability analysis for sustainability strategic business decisions.

For organizations reporting under the European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS) or implementing IFRS Sustainability Disclosure Standards, reporting requirements are increasingly interconnected across frameworks. Consequently, interoperability is considered a critical enabler for organizations to align sustainability data across multiple regulatory and voluntary standards. SAP Sustainability solutions adopt interoperability as a characteristic for companies reporting under multiple frameworks, which can increasingly consolidate their sustainability data management rather than duplicating effort across disconnected processes.

End-to-end sustainability reporting requires an auditable chain from operational cause through identification, collection, calculation, analysis, and disclosure. Point tools own a slice of that chain, while SAP owns the whole of it. SAP Sustainability Control Tower and SAP Sustainability Footprint Management together enable an end‑to‑end IFRS S1 and S2 sustainability reporting flow, including carbon footprint calculation, and climate- and sustainability-related data acquisition through to governed disclosures. SAP Sustainability Control Tower now provides SAP‑delivered IFRS S1 and S2 data points as master content, so organizations can manage IFRS S1 and S2 disclosures within the same governance framework they already use for ESRS reporting, while SAP Sustainability Footprint Management supplies the underlying emissions and activity data needed for IFRS S2 climate‑related metrics. This post walks through the integrated flow from initial setup and data integration through to AI‑assisted report creation.

Initial Setup and Master Data

The starting point for IFRS S1 and S2 reporting in SAP Sustainability Control Tower is the Manage Master Data application. Here, organizations configure the foundational structures that underpin their sustainability disclosures, including reporting structures such as legal entities, business locations, and organizational units, as well as the associated hierarchies that define the reporting boundary.

Now, the reporting requirements under IFRS S1 and S2, version 2023, are provided by SAP in the “Reporting Standard”, “Reporting Standard Version,” and “Data Points” dimensions in the Manage Master Data App as of July 1st, 2026.

For IFRS reporting specifically, the same organizational reporting structure used to support ESRS disclosures is reused. This means organizations already configured for CSRD reporting do not need to rebuild their hierarchy levels, fiscal year variants, and organizational mappings, providing a unified data foundation across both ESRS and IFRS disclosure requirements.

Metrics Coverage

In the Manage Metrics application, organizations can now access SAP-provided metrics mapped to IFRS S1 and S2 data points.

As of July 2026, SAP Sustainability Control Tower includes:

  • 24 quantitative metrics for IFRS S2 Climate-Related Disclosures, covering greenhouse gas emissions (Scope 1, 2, and 3) and carbon credits..
  • 57 qualitative metrics across IFRS S1 and S2, including:
    • IFRS S1 General Disclosures: 13 metrics
    • IFRS S1 and IFRS S2 shared General Disclosures: 15 metrics
    • IFRS S2 Climate-Related Disclosures: 29 metrics

To support interoperability, qualitative metrics that appear in both IFRS S1 and IFRS S2 are represented as a single metric where applicable. This avoids duplicating data entry for disclosures that serve both standards.

Data points that include explanatory content, implementation guidance, or reporting clarifications are out of scope and are not included in the delivered master data. Organizations can refer to the corresponding IFRS standards documentation for this information.

Within metric disclosure references, customers can see, when applicable, interoperability between disclosure requirements across standards such as ESRS and IFRS, helping organizations address multiple reporting frameworks through a single reporting effort.

Reporting Scope

Once metrics are available, organizations define their reporting scope: which material metrics apply to which parts of their reporting structure, and for which periods. The reporting scope configuration in SAP Sustainability Control Tower allows organizations to select IFRS-relevant metrics alongside their existing ESRS scope.

This is particularly relevant for organizations reporting under both ESRS and IFRS, where many climate-related disclosures overlap. Because SAP Sustainability Control Tower supports interoperability with standards in its metric definitions, organizations can configure their reporting scope once and satisfy data requirements for multiple frameworks without managing parallel reporting processes.

Data Acquisition

With the reporting scope defined, data acquisition follows established SAP Sustainability Control Tower patterns. Quantitative data for IFRS S2 climate metrics can be sourced through the same channels used for ESRS climate data:

  • SAP Sustainability Footprint Management integration for greenhouse gas emissions data across scope 1, 2 and 3, with configurable period granularity (monthly, quarterly, yearly) based on the active fiscal year variant.
  • SAP Sustainability Footprint Management energy and fuel mix metrics for IFRS‑relevant climate information, adding energy consumption, energy mix, fuel mix, energy content and sourcing type, calculated together with the emissions in a single run.
  • SAP Datasphere content packages for loading actuals from connected source systems.
  • File upload for data not available through system integration.
  • Inbound ODATA API for programmatic data ingestion from any source.

For qualitative metrics, the data collection process supports form-based collection with workflow governance. Organizations can group IFRS qualitative metrics within a single data collection form, assign processors and approvers, and manage the entire collection cycle through governed workflows. It also supports collection of the corporate summary while showing previously recorded data for comparison.

Emissions and Energy Data

For IFRS S2 greenhouse gas disclosures, SAP Sustainability Footprint Management calculates corporate emissions directly based on ERP master and transactional data, rather than from manual uploads or separate data silos. This creates one governed data foundation for Scope 1, 2 and 3 results that aligns climate metrics with the same operational events and structures used to run the business.

In the same calculation flow, the solution can also deliver energy‑related metrics such as energy consumption, energy mix, fuel mix, energy content and sourcing type, where these are relevant for IFRS S2 reporting. One run of the model, therefore, produces multiple climate‑related outputs: mandatory emissions data plus optional energy metrics to support transition analysis and target tracking.

Because activity data, emission factors and calculation logic are all traceable back to their source, the resulting IFRS S2 figures are easier to substantiate. When transferred into SAP Sustainability Control Tower via direct integration, this governance and lineage are preserved, connecting operational cause, calculation and disclosure in a single, auditable chain - eliminating the need for external transformation or aggregation steps.

Note: SAP Sustainability Control Tower's emissions-related Data Provider Interfaces (including SAP_SCT_DPI_Emission and SAP_SCT_DPI_Energy) provide the structure for ingesting this data from SAP and non-SAP sources.

Analytics

Analyze ESG Data application enables organizations to explore their IFRS-aligned sustainability performance. With the target-versus-actual visualization capabilities delivered in Q2 2026, organizations can compare their climate-related performance against defined targets directly within the application.

For IFRS S2, this is particularly relevant for transition plan monitoring: organizations can track progress toward their greenhouse gas reduction targets, visualize emissions trends across reporting periods, and drill down by reporting structure to identify areas requiring attention.

The flexible chart-specific configuration model allows independent control over metric selection, filters, drilldowns, and chart types. Users can display up to six charts in parallel and combine chart and table views for side-by-side analysis of different IFRS disclosure dimensions, such as comparing Scope 1, 2, and 3 emissions performance across legal entities or time periods.

 

AI-Assisted Report Generation

Generate Sustainability Reports with AI is available free of charge to all SAP Sustainability Control Tower customers as a base AI feature. Today, customers can already use the Generic ESG Reporting Template to automatically draft ESG reports in multiple languages, preview and edit the content, and download the result in PDF or DOCX format, with dynamic AI‑driven revisions helping refine the final narrative.

Building on these capabilities, the Generate ESG Reports with AI application will include an IFRS‑specific report template as a roadmap item for H2 2026. This template will allow organizations to generate a structured IFRS sustainability disclosure report from the quantitative and qualitative data managed in SAP Sustainability Control Tower, drawing on the governed ESG data foundation to produce a draft aligned with IFRS S1 and S2 requirements. Using the IFRS template, AI‑assisted report generation will cover the core IFRS content pillars—Governance, Strategy, Risk Management, and Metrics and Targets—providing a standards‑aligned starting point that customers can further tailor to their specific context.

 Interoperability: ESRS and IFRS Side by Side

A key design principle behind the IFRS content in SAP Sustainability Control Tower is interoperability. Organizations reporting under both ESRS (for CSRD compliance) and IFRS (for jurisdictions adopting ISSB standards) can manage both from a single data foundation.

Where disclosure requirements overlap, particularly in general disclosures and climate-related reporting, SAP Sustainability Control Tower's metric definitions are designed so that data entered once can satisfy requirements across both frameworks. Within the metric general information, organizations can see the mapping between ESRS and IFRS disclosure requirements, reducing the effort required to maintain parallel reporting tracks.

Additional Information

Documentation on IFRS S1 and S2 metrics is available in SAP Help Portal for SAP Sustainability Control Tower.

Scenario Guidance for Corporate Carbon Calculation is available in SAP Help Portal for SAP Sustainability Footprint Management.

entry.title: Dangerous Goods Multi-Option Packing Instructions and Migration Support
entry.content:
In the world of dangerous goods compliance, precision and flexibility go hand in hand. With the latest innovations closely aligned to the UN Model Regulations, we’re introducing practical enhancements that make it easier to model regulations as they’re written—and operationalize them in your processes.
 

What’s new

  • Multiple combination packaging options in one packing instruction
    • Some packing instructions now include two or more valid combination packaging options—just as the regulations allow.
    • Example: P400 can present two distinct options, both visible and selectable directly in the system.

 

Within the View Regulatory Data - Dangerous Goods app, users can choose a specific UN entry and see all DG regulations linked to that UN number in one overview. You can then drill down to details, including the multi-option packing instruction view.

Why it matters

  • Reflects real-world regulatory nuance
    • Many country/authority implementations are close to the UN model. Where the model offers multiple choices, your master data can now reflect that without workarounds.
  • Reduces ambiguity and rework
    • Clear visibility of every valid combination option helps regulatory teams and logistics planners converge on the right packaging configuration faster.
  • Improves auditability
    • The system shows the available options and your choice, making it easier to demonstrate due diligence during reviews.

Migration cockpit support: loading DG classifications for packing instructions

To speed up onboarding and harmonization, we’ve added migration cockpit support to load dangerous goods classifications for packing instructions.
  • Key points
    • You must load the packing instruction itself before you load product-specific assessments for that packing instruction.
    • Determination records can be loaded in any sequence relative to the assessments—the critical precondition is: the packing instruction exists first.
    • The migration template mirrors the familiar fields from product master classification migration—with one important difference: the key is the packing instruction, not the product master.

Getting started

  • Review your current DG master data model and identify where multiple combination options apply (e.g., P400).
  • Prepare migration templates:
    • Packing instructions first
    • Then assessments for product-in-packing-instruction
  • Validate with a representative UN number and walk through the in-app overview and details to confirm your data behaves as expected.

FAQs

  • Can I rely on the system to display all relevant options for a given packing instruction?
    • Yes, when multiple options are defined (e.g., P400), they are shown explicitly to help you make the right selection.
  • What happens if I load assessments before the packing instruction?
    • The assessments won’t resolve properly. Ensure packing instructions are loaded first.
  • Is the determination record load order strict?
    • No. The load order of determination records relative to assessments is flexible—as long as the packing instruction is already in place.

entry.title: What Does It Mean to Be an Expert in the Age of Agentic AI and the Autonomous Enterprise? - Part 1/3
entry.content:
For many years, learning in enterprise software has followed a fairly predictable pattern.
A new regulation appears. A new product feature is released. A new business process is introduced or amended to integrate the new requirements. Training helps people understand it, use it (implement, administer, position, develop etc) and ultimately become experts in its application.
That model has served us well.
But as AI agents and assistants, within the context of the Autonomous Enterprise, become part of everyday work, something more fundamental is beginning to change.
It is no longer just what we need to learn that is evolving. It is what it means to be an expert.
From remembering to reasoning
For decades, expertise often meant knowing more than everyone else. You knew the regulations. You understood the configuration. You remembered the transaction codes. You could explain complex reporting rules from memory. Agentic AI is changing this.
Employees are increasingly gaining immediate access to agents and assistants capable of retrieving legislation, explaining product functionality, summarising guidance and generating first drafts of reports in seconds.
Knowledge itself and that particular knowledge we need available to us for our jobs becomes dramatically more accessible.
That doesn't make expertise less valuable, but it changes where expertise lies and where the central locus of that expertise needs to be.
The competitive advantage increasingly moves from remembering information towards asking better questions, challenging assumptions, recognising exceptions and making sound business judgements in the face of competing priorities and trade-offs.
Perhaps, therefore, the expert of the future is not primarily the person who always knows the answer. Instead perhaps It is the person who knows what question to ask, how to evaluate the answer, and when the answer doesn't quite make sense. And for sustainability professionals, (including those for whom sustainability was not traditionally a concern, such as finance professionals) that shift may be particularly important.
Because another change is happening at the same time: sustainability itself is moving from the edges of the enterprise towards the centre of operational decision-making.
In the next blog: What happens when sustainability moves from reporting what happened to helping decide what should happen next?

entry.title: What Does It Mean to Be an Expert in the Age of Agentic AI and the Autonomous Enterprise? Part2/3
entry.content:
Historically, sustainability has often been treated as a reporting exercise. Data was collected. Reports were produced. Compliance obligations were fulfilled.


Increasingly, sustainability data and information is becoming embedded directly into core ERP processes. Carbon emissions, packaging obligations, product compliance, Extended Producer Responsibility, CBAM exposure and many other sustainability dimensions are becoming part of operational decision-making rather than simply end-of-year or quarter reporting.
Instead of asking, "What happened last quarter?" organisations will increasingly ask: "What should we be doing next?"
And here AI can help evaluate thousands of possible options, but with humans still deciding which objectives matter most.
From systems of record to systems of reasoning


Imagine being able to ask, "How can we reduce packaging costs while remaining compliant with PPWR and maintaining customer satisfaction?" Or "Which suppliers create the greatest carbon risk if we move production to a different region?"
Instead of manually gathering information from multiple systems, AI assistants will increasingly assemble the relevant data, explain the trade-offs and propose recommendations.


In many situations, specialist AI agents will even be able to perform the analysis continuously in the background and in real time.
This changes the role of sustainability information, so that It is no longer simply evidence of what the organisation has done. It becomes an input into what the organisation should do next.
So what then happens to human expertise? Can’t we give all this sustainability activity over to the AI and take a coffee break?
This does not mean AI replaces sustainability professionals. Quite the opposite.
As AI takes over routine information gathering and analysis within predefined guardrails, human expertise becomes more valuable in areas where judgement is essential.


Consider questions (more questions!) such as:
• Which recommendation best aligns with company strategy?
• Are we optimising for cost at the expense of resilience?
• What are the CBAM implications of this aluminium sourcing plan, and how will that affect margin?
• Does this recommendation satisfy both regulators and customers?
• Are there ethical consequences beyond legal compliance?
• Should we accept the AI's recommendation — or challenge it?
These remain fundamentally human decisions.
(Perhaps one of the most important skills in an AI-enabled enterprise will therefore be knowing when not to trust the first answer!)
And there is another consequence.


Sustainability considerations increasingly become integrated into business activities within the purview of the CFO, COO and CEO — not just the Chief Sustainability Officer (and if your ‘C’ area is not listed here, then probably you too. 😊).
The sustainability professional therefore becomes less of a specialist operating at the edge of the business and more of someone helping the organisation understand and orchestrate complex trade-offs across it.
But this raises a very important question. If this is how people will work, are we training the right people and are we teaching them the right things?
That's the subject of the final blog.

entry.title: Learning Sustainability in the Age of AI (Pt 3/3)
entry.content:
If work changes, learning must change with it. Traditional enterprise learning often focused on teaching users every detail of a system. Future learning for sustainability may need to focus more on:
• understanding business concepts rather than memorising transactions
• working effectively with AI assistants
• managing trade-offs between competing environmental, financial, social and risk objectives
• supervising AI agents rather than manually completing every task
• interpreting recommendations instead of simply generating reports
• understanding the quality and provenance of data
• recognising bias, uncertainty and missing context
• making decisions where there is no single "correct" answer
In other words, learning becomes less about navigation and more about judgement.
But what should learners learn today and how do you prepare for the direction of travel?
Nobody knows exactly how quickly these changes will arrive. But there are several capabilities that are already worth developing. And these are just my unofficial list!
• Be curious beyond your own functional area.
Sustainability increasingly connects finance, procurement, manufacturing, logistics, product compliance and product design. Understanding those connections becomes increasingly important.
• Learn the underlying business concepts, not just the software.
If AI can increasingly help us navigate software, understanding what the process is trying to achieve — and why — becomes even more valuable.
• Experiment with SAP Joule and SAP AI assistants.
Learning how to ask good questions may become just as valuable as learning where information is stored.

• Develop critical thinking.
AI can produce convincing answers very quickly. Understanding when to question those answers will remain essential.
• Become comfortable with trade-offs.
Many sustainability decisions involve balancing cost, carbon, compliance, resilience and customer expectations. Future professionals will increasingly orchestrate these competing objectives rather than optimise only one.
Looking ahead (though not an official SAP prediction)
No one can predict exactly what enterprise work will look like five years from now, but what seems increasingly likely is that AI will become another member of the team.
Some AI will answer questions. Some AI will perform analysis. Some AI agents will coordinate work across multiple business processes.
The most successful professionals will not simply know more.
They will know how to work effectively alongside intelligent systems, understand the business context in which those systems operate, and exercise the judgement that only humans can provide — within the organisational guardrails defined for the Autonomous Enterprise.
The future of learning is therefore not about competing with AI. It is about learning how to think with it.

entry.title: Green Ledger in eCommerce CX: Integrating SAP Commerce Cloud with SAP Sustainability Control Tower
entry.content:
Sustainability information is increasingly relevant to purchasing decisions, but a digital storefront can only communicate it responsibly when the underlying data is traceable, consistently calculated, and presented with the correct context.

"Only by moving from averages to actuals — audited at reasonable assurance — can freeriding and greenwashing be avoided, thereby protecting such valuable investment and our planet."

— Dominik Asam, CFO, SAP SE (December 2024)

Many commerce experiences still rely on broad statements such as “sustainably made” or “environmentally friendly.” These statements may communicate intent, but they do not explain what was measured, which lifecycle boundary was used, when the calculation was performed, or where the data originated.

A more transparent approach is to treat a product carbon footprint as governed product data. Instead of adding another marketing message to the product page, the commerce platform presents an approved carbon value together with its unit, calculation boundary, source, reporting period, and methodology.

This article presents a solution blueprint for bringing product carbon footprint information into . The proposed architecture uses product footprint information calculated and published through SAP sustainability solutions, an integration and mediation layer on , and the extensibility of  and Composable Storefront.

 

That gap is now closeable.

Table of Contents:

  • 1. Introduction: From carbon accounting to the digital storefront
  • 2. Roles of the SAP solutions
  • SAP Green Ledger
  • SAP Sustainability Footprint Management
  • SAP Sustainability Control Tower
  • SAP Business Technology Platform
  • 3. The most important prerequisite: a common product identifier
  • 4. Integration and consumption patterns
  • Pattern A: Scheduled synchronization
  • Pattern B: Runtime carbon-data facade
  • Pattern C: Hybrid model
  • 5. Modelling carbon information in SAP Commerce Cloud
  • 6. Storefront experience patterns
  • Product detail page
  • Search and category pages
  • Cart and checkout
  • Customer sustainability view
  • 7. Handling missing, stale, or incomparable data
  • 8. Transparency and green-claims controls
  • 9. Operational controls
  • 10. A practical implementation sequence with examples
  • SAP Landscape Prerequisites
  • Data Prerequisites — The Product ID Bridge
  • Integration Architecture & Code Examples
  • Layer 2 — Calling the SFM Published Product Footprints API
  • Layer 3 — BTP iFlow: Groovy Mapping Script
  • Layer 3 — Commerce Cloud ImpEx: Custom Product Type Extension
  • Layer 4 — Composable Storefront: Carbon Badge Angular Component
  • Layer 4 — Cart CO₂e Aggregation Service
  • Layer 3 — Real-Time Facade: BTP CAP Microservice
  • Key patterns
  • Pattern A — Carbon Badge on the PDP
  • Pattern B — Carbon Sort and Filter in Search
  • Pattern C — Cart Carbon Summary
  • Pattern D — My Sustainability Account Dashboard
  • Conclusion

Important: The architecture and examples in this article are illustrative. They should be adapted to the APIs, data contracts, product versions, extension mechanisms, security requirements, and sustainability-governance policies applicable to the implementation.

 

1. Introduction: From carbon accounting to the digital storefront

The central idea is straightforward: carbon information that is already calculated and governed in enterprise systems can also be consumed by customer-facing applications.

In this blueprint, the sustainability and commerce landscape has four logical layers:

  1. Data production: Operational, financial, material, energy, and supplier information provides the basis for sustainability calculations.
  2. Data publication: Approved product footprint information is made available through a supported outbound interface.
  3. Data mediation: An integration service validates identifiers, transforms units and structures, applies publication rules, and protects the source system from storefront traffic.
  4. Data consumption: SAP Commerce Cloud exposes the information through product, search, cart, and account experiences

This separation is important. The storefront should consume approved sustainability information, but it should not become the system in which the footprint is calculated or certified.

 

2. Roles of the SAP solutions

SAP Green Ledger

SAP Green Ledger connects carbon information with financial and operational dimensions. In the context of this blueprint, it represents the accounting and allocation perspective behind enterprise carbon management

The design should not assume that SAP Green Ledger directly supplies a storefront-specific payload. The commerce integration consumes an approved product footprint from the designated publication layer in the customer landscape.

SAP Sustainability Footprint Management

SAP Sustainability Footprint Management is the product-footprint calculation and management component in this scenario. It can calculate corporate and product footprints using operational data, material flows, energy information, supplier data, and applicable emission factors.

SFM now supports publishing product carbon footprints on the outbound side via an API available on SAP Business Accelerator Hub — Published Product Footprints — through which any consuming application can retrieve footprints for carbon data exchange. Publishing applies to finished and semi-finished products and supports the PACT consortium's format (version 2.1.0). This API is the cornerstone of the entire integration.

Only a footprint that has passed the organization’s review and publication controls should become eligible for downstream commerce use.

SAP Sustainability Control Tower

SAP Sustainability Control Tower supports enterprise-wide sustainability performance management and reporting. It provides the broader sustainability-management context, while the product-facing experience relies on the approved data source selected by the implementation

SAP Business Technology Platform

SAP Business Technology Platform provides the integration and extension foundation. Depending on the architecture, this layer can perform orchestration, authentication, transformation, validation, caching, monitoring, and exception handling

Keeping these responsibilities outside the storefront creates a cleaner separation between calculation, governance, integration, and customer experience.

 

3. The most important prerequisite: a common product identifier

The integration depends on the ability to match a footprint record to the correct commerce product. A shared identifier is therefore the most important data prerequisite.

Depending on the landscape, the linking value might be an ERP material number, a GTIN, or another governed identifier. The exact key is less important than its consistency and uniqueness across the participating systems.

Before implementation begins, the project team should establish:

  • Which identifier is authoritative.
  • Where it is stored in SAP Commerce Cloud.
  • How it is represented in the published footprint data.
  • Whether the same identifier can represent variants, units, or packaging levels.
  • How duplicate, missing, or obsolete mappings will be handled.

A coverage assessment should then identify which online products have a valid mapping and an approved footprint. This prevents the storefront from displaying incomplete or incorrectly associated information.

 

4. Integration and consumption patterns

The appropriate consumption model depends on footprint update frequency, storefront traffic, latency expectations, and operational-governance requirements.

Pattern A: Scheduled synchronization

A scheduled integration flow retrieves approved footprint records and writes selected values into custom product attributes in SAP Commerce Cloud.

This pattern is suitable when footprints change less frequently and the storefront requires fast local access. The synchronized attributes can also be indexed to support search, filtering, and sorting.

The synchronization process should be idempotent and should retain the source identifier, source timestamp, declared unit, footprint boundary, and methodology reference. Failed or ambiguous mappings should be logged for review rather than silently imported.

Pattern B: Runtime carbon-data facade

A service on SAP BTP can act as a controlled facade between the storefront and the sustainability source. SAP Commerce Cloud requests the footprint using the governed product identifier, and the facade returns a storefront-oriented response.

The facade can centralize authentication, mapping, unit normalization, caching, and error handling. It can also prevent direct customer traffic from reaching the footprint-calculation system.

This pattern may be appropriate when approved footprint data changes more frequently or when storing the data in SAP Commerce Cloud is not desired.

Pattern C: Hybrid model

A hybrid design can synchronize the primary value and publication metadata into SAP Commerce Cloud while retrieving additional methodology or lifecycle details on demand.

This provides fast product-page rendering while keeping detailed information governed by the sustainability-data service.

 

5. Modelling carbon information in SAP Commerce Cloud

The commerce data model should contain only the attributes required by the approved customer experience. A practical model could include:

  • Footprint value.
  • Declared unit.
  • Footprint or lifecycle boundary.
  • Source system or dataset identifier.
  • Methodology or specification reference.
  • Reporting-period end or publication date.
  • Last synchronization timestamp.
  • Publication or display eligibility.

The field names and types must be aligned with the actual source contract. The storefront should not reinterpret a field or describe it as Scope 1, Scope 2, or Scope 3 unless the source explicitly supplies that classification for the displayed product footprint.

Similarly, a “low carbon” badge should not be generated from an arbitrary universal threshold. If such a badge is introduced, its comparison population, threshold, category, geography, validity period, and approval process must be defined and governed.

 

6. Storefront experience patterns

Once the footprint is available as governed commerce data, it can support several customer-experience patterns.

Product detail page

The product page can display the carbon footprint value per declared unit, together with the calculation boundary, data source, methodology reference, and relevant date.

A concise summary can be visible by default, with detailed methodology information presented in an expandable panel. This helps keep the page understandable without hiding the basis of the claim.

Below is a visual example created for education purposes with randomized data:

Product Display Page with Carbon footprint information and sustainability touchpoints

Search and category pages

 

Where product coverage and unit comparability are sufficient, the footprint can be indexed for search experiences such as:

  • Displaying carbon information on product cards.
  • Filtering to products with published footprint information.
  • Sorting comparable products by footprint value.

Sorting should only be enabled where the compared values use compatible declared units and boundaries. A raw numeric sort across incomparable product types could mislead customers.

Cart and checkout

A cart-level summary can aggregate product footprint values by multiplying the approved per-unit value by the ordered quantity.

However, the total should clearly indicate coverage. If only some cart items have published data, the experience should not present the partial value as the footprint of the complete cart.

Below is a visual example created for education purposes with randomized data:

Cart page with Carbon footprint information and sustainability touchpoints

Customer sustainability view

 

A customer account could provide an optional view of footprint information associated with previous purchases. This would require the relevant value and methodology metadata to be retained with the order entry so that historical results are not changed by later product-data updates.

This pattern also requires appropriate privacy, retention, accessibility, and customer-consent review.

 

7. Handling missing, stale, or incomparable data

A responsible design must define what happens when the ideal data is unavailable.

  • Missing footprint: Do not display zero. Zero is a measurement and must not be used as a substitute for unavailable data.
  • Missing identifier: Exclude the record from publication and route it for data-quality review.
  • Stale data: Apply an agreed validity rule and display the relevant reporting or publication date.
  • Unit mismatch: Do not aggregate or rank values until a governed conversion is available.
  • Calculation-boundary mismatch: Do not present the values as directly comparable.
  • Integration failure: Preserve the last approved value only if the governance policy permits it and its date remains visible.

 

8. Transparency and green-claims controls

Displaying a carbon number does not by itself establish a responsible environmental claim. The implementation should preserve enough metadata for the claim to be understood and reviewed.

At a minimum, the customer experience should consider displaying:

  • The numerical value and declared unit.
  • The relevant lifecycle or calculation boundary.
  • The source or calculation system.
  • The reporting period or publication date.
  • The methodology or specification used.
  • A coverage statement where the experience aggregates multiple products.

Contextual equivalents, rankings, offsets, badges, and comparative claims introduce further assumptions. They should only be enabled after the underlying factor, comparison set, calculation method, and approval process have been documented and reviewed.

 

9. Operational controls

The integration should be operated as a governed data product rather than as a one-time storefront enhancement.

Recommended controls include:

  • Authentication and authorization between every system boundary.
  • Secrets and destination management outside application code.
  • Schema and unit validation before publication.
  • Idempotent updates and controlled retry handling.
  • Monitoring for failed, stale, duplicate, and unmapped records.
  • Auditability from the storefront value to the source footprint record.
  • Business ownership for badge, ranking, and publication rules.
  • Legal and sustainability review of customer-facing environmental claims.

These controls ensure that the customer experience remains aligned with the approved data even as products, calculations, and source systems change.

 

10. A practical implementation sequence with examples

The implementation should ideally have the below sequence:

  1. Confirm the approved sustainability-data source and outbound interface.
  2. Define the customer-facing use case and required metadata.
  3. Establish the common product identifier and assess catalogue coverage.
  4. Validate units, boundaries, reporting periods, and publication status.
  5. Select the scheduled, runtime, or hybrid integration pattern.
  6. Extend the SAP Commerce Cloud data and API models where required.
  7. Implement the product-page experience before adding comparison or aggregation features.
  8. Add monitoring, reconciliation, and exception handling.
  9. Complete sustainability, legal, accessibility, security, and performance reviews.
  10. Pilot with a controlled product set before extending coverage.

SAP Landscape Prerequisites

Prerequisite

Detail

SAP Commerce Cloud (CCv2)

Version 2211+; Composable Storefront (Spartacus 6+) preferred for API-first consumption

SAP S/4HANA Cloud

ERP backbone for SAP Green Ledger and SFM

SAP Sustainability Footprint Management

Active subscription; products published via Publish Product Footprints app with "Published" status

SAP Sustainability Control Tower

Active subscription; SFM integration configured via BTP destination

SAP Business Technology Platform (BTP)

Required for Green Ledger (BTP app); Integration Suite for mediation layer

SAP Business Accelerator Hub

For consuming Published Product Footprints API and SustainabilityCustomMetricsData API

Data Prerequisites — The Product ID Bridge

The single most critical data prerequisite is a shared product identifier between Commerce Cloud and SFM. In most SAP landscapes this is the ERP material number, which already exists in both systems. This is the linking key across the entire integration.

A practical data validation query to run in your SAP Commerce Cloud Backoffice before build:

-- Run in SAP Commerce Cloud Flexible Search to identify products that have an ERP material number mapped
SELECT {p:code}, {p:name[en]}, {p:erpMaterialNumber}
FROM {Product AS p}
WHERE {p:erpMaterialNumber} IS NOT NULL
  AND {p:catalogVersion} = (
    SELECT {cv:pk} FROM {CatalogVersion AS cv}
    WHERE {cv:version} = 'Online'
  )
ORDER BY {p:code}

This gives you the coverage map — products eligible for carbon data enrichment on day one.

Integration Architecture & Code Examples

The integration operates across four layers:

  1. Layer 1 - data production,
  2. Layer 2 - data publication,
  3. Layer 3 - data mediation,
  4. Layer 4 - data consumption

Post data production in Layer 1, let's go layer by layer with implementation details.

Layer 2 — Calling the SFM Published Product Footprints API

The Published Product Footprints API on SAP Business Accelerator Hub returns PCF data in PACT v2.1.0 format. Here is a representative call and response structure:

// BTP Integration Suite iFlow — Node.js-style pseudocode
// Calling the SAP SFM Published Product Footprints API

const SFM_PCF_API = 'https://<sfm-tenant>.cfapps.<region>.hana.ondemand.com';
const API_PATH    = '/api/v1/productfootprints';

async function fetchProductFootprints(accessToken, materialNumbers) {
  const filter = materialNumbers
    .map(n => `productId eq '${n}'`)
    .join(' or ');

  const response = await fetch(
    `${SFM_PCF_API}${API_PATH}?$filter=(${filter})&$format=json`,
    {
      method: 'GET',
      headers: {
        'Authorization': `Bearer ${accessToken}`,
        'Accept':        'application/json',
        'DataModelVersion': '2.1.0'  // PACT v2.1 header
      }
    }
  );

  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error(`SFM API error: ${response.status}`);
  }
  return response.json();
}
A representative PACT v2.1 response payload looks like this:
{
  "data": [
    {
      "id": "3893bb5d-da16-4dc1-9185-11d97476c254",
      "specVersion": "2.1.0",
      "version": 1,
      "status": "Active",
      "companyName": "AcmeCorp AG",
      "productNameCompany": "Trail Runner Pro X2",
      "productIds": ["urn:gtin:40712345678906"],
      "productCategoryCpc": "56112",
      "reportingPeriodStart": "2024-01-01T00:00:00Z",
      "reportingPeriodEnd":   "2024-12-31T23:59:59Z",
      "pcf": {
        "declaredUnit": "piece",
        "unitaryProductAmount": "1",
        "pCfExcludingBiogenic": "6.2",
        "fossilGhgEmissions": "5.8",
        "biogenicCarbonWithdrawal": "0.4",
        "dLucGhgEmissions": "0",
        "landManagementGhgEmissions": "0",
        "otherBiogenicGhgEmissions": "0",
        "geographyCountrySubdivision": "DE",
        "referencePeriodStart": "2024-01-01T00:00:00Z",
        "referencePeriodEnd":   "2024-12-31T23:59:59Z",
        "characterizationFactors": "AR6",
        "boundaryProcessesDescription": "Cradle-to-gate, PACT v2.1",
        "crossSectoralStandardsUsed": ["GHG Protocol Product standard"],
        "exemptedEmissionsPercent": 0
      }
    }
  ]
}

The key field for the storefront is pcf.pCfExcludingBiogenic — the CO₂e value per declared unit.

Layer 3 — BTP iFlow: Groovy Mapping Script

Inside the SAP BTP Integration Suite iFlow, a Groovy script maps SFM footprint values to Commerce Cloud product attributes. This runs as part of the Message Mapping step:

// BTP Integration Suite — Groovy Script (Message Mapping)
// Maps SFM PACT v2.1 response → Commerce Cloud product attribute payload

import groovy.json.JsonSlurper
import groovy.json.JsonOutput

def Message processData(Message message) {
    def body    = message.getBody(String)
    def slurper = new JsonSlurper()
    def sfmData = slurper.parseText(body)

    def commercePayload = []

    sfmData.data.each { footprint ->
        // Extract the GTIN and strip the URN prefix
        def gtin = footprint.productIds
            ?.find { it.startsWith('urn:gtin:') }
            ?.replace('urn:gtin:', '') ?: null

        if (!gtin) return  // skip if no GTIN linkage

        def co2eValue = footprint.pcf?.pCfExcludingBiogenic?.toBigDecimal()
        def scope1    = footprint.pcf?.fossilGhgEmissions?.toBigDecimal()  ?: 0
        def lastUpdate = footprint.reportingPeriodEnd

        // Badge eligibility threshold — configurable
        // Products below 8.0 kgCO2e/unit receive "Low Carbon" badge
        def LOW_CARBON_THRESHOLD = 8.0
        def isLowCarbon = co2eValue != null && co2eValue < LOW_CARBON_THRESHOLD

        commercePayload << [
            erpMaterialNumber      : gtin,
            carbonFootprintKgCO2e  : co2eValue,
            carbonScope1KgCO2e     : scope1,
            carbonDataSource       : "SAP-SFM-PACT-v2.1",
            carbonLastUpdated      : lastUpdate,
            carbonLowCarbonBadge   : isLowCarbon,
            carbonBoundary         : footprint.pcf?.boundaryProcessesDescription,
            carbonPactVersion      : footprint.specVersion
        ]
    }

    message.setBody(JsonOutput.toJson([products: commercePayload]))
    return message
}

 

Layer 3 — Commerce Cloud ImpEx: Custom Product Type Extension

Before the iFlow can write carbon data into SAP Commerce Cloud, the product type must be extended to accept these attributes. This is done via ImpEx, the standard Commerce Cloud import mechanism:

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------
# SAP Commerce Cloud — Carbon Footprint Product Attribute Extension
# File: carbon-footprint-extension.impex
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------

# 1. Extend the Product type with carbon attributes
INSERT_UPDATE AttributeDescriptor; enclosingType(code)[unique=true]; qualifier[unique=true]; type(code); generate; search; optional; defaultValue
; Product ; carbonFootprintKgCO2e  ; java.lang.Double  ; true ; true  ; true ;
; Product ; carbonScope1KgCO2e     ; java.lang.Double  ; true ; false ; true ;
; Product ; carbonDataSource       ; java.lang.String  ; true ; false ; true ;
; Product ; carbonLastUpdated      ; java.util.Date    ; true ; false ; true ;
; Product ; carbonLowCarbonBadge   ; java.lang.Boolean ; true ; true  ; true ; false
; Product ; carbonBoundary         ; java.lang.String  ; true ; false ; true ;
; Product ; carbonPactVersion      ; java.lang.String  ; true ; false ; true ;

# 2. Make carbonFootprintKgCO2e searchable in Solr for facet/sort
INSERT_UPDATE SolrIndexedProperty; solrIndexedType(identifier)[unique=true]; name[unique=true]; type(code); sortableType(code); currency[default=false]; localized[default=false]; multiValue[default=false]; useForSpellchecking[default=false]; useForAutocomplete[default=false]
; electronicsProductType ; carbonFootprintKgCO2e ; double ; ;  ;  ;  ;  ;
; electronicsProductType ; carbonLowCarbonBadge  ; boolean ; ;  ;  ;  ;  ;

# 3. Add carbon sort configuration
INSERT_UPDATE SolrSortField; sort(indexedType(identifier),code)[unique=true]; fieldName[unique=true]; ascending[unique=true]
; electronicsProductType:carbon-asc  ; carbonFootprintKgCO2e ; true
; electronicsProductType:carbon-desc ; carbonFootprintKgCO2e ; false

INSERT_UPDATE SolrSort; indexedType(identifier)[unique=true]; code[unique=true]; name[lang=en]
; electronicsProductType ; carbon-asc  ; Carbon footprint: low to high
; electronicsProductType ; carbon-desc ; Carbon footprint: high to low

This creates the database columns, makes the footprint value Solr-indexed (enabling sorting and faceting), and adds "Carbon footprint: low to high" as a native sort option in search.

Layer 4 — Composable Storefront: Carbon Badge Angular Component

The storefront integration lives in a custom Spartacus feature module. Here is the Angular component that renders the carbon badge seen in the PDP mockup above:

// carbon-badge.component.ts
// SAP Composable Storefront (Spartacus) — Carbon Footprint Feature Module

import { Component, Input, OnInit } from '@angular/core';
import { Product } from '@spartacus/core';

export interface CarbonFootprintData {
  co2eKg:         number;
  scope1Kg:       number;
  dataSource:     string;
  lastUpdated:    string;
  isLowCarbon:    boolean;
  boundary:       string;
  pactVersion:    string;
}

@Component({
  selector: 'app-carbon-badge',
  template: `
    <div *ngIf="carbon" class="carbon-badge-container">

      <!-- Low Carbon chip (conditionally rendered) -->
      <div *ngIf="carbon.isLowCarbon" class="low-carbon-chip">
        <span class="chip-icon">✓</span> Low carbon
      </div>

      <!-- Main CO₂e value -->
      <div class="co2-display">
        <span class="co2-value">{{ carbon.co2eKg | number:'1.1-1' }}</span>
        <span class="co2-unit">kgCO₂e / unit</span>
      </div>

      <!-- Contextual equivalent -->
      <div class="co2-equivalent">
        ≈ Driving {{ drivingEquivalentKm | number:'1.0-0' }} km in a petrol car
      </div>

      <!-- Expandable methodology panel -->
      <button class="methodology-toggle" (click)="showMethodology = !showMethodology">
        How is this calculated? {{ showMethodology ? '↑' : '↓' }}
      </button>

      <div *ngIf="showMethodology" class="methodology-panel">
        <p><strong>Lifecycle boundary:</strong> {{ carbon.boundary }}</p>
        <p><strong>Standard:</strong> PACT v{{ carbon.pactVersion }}</p>
        <p><strong>Data source:</strong> {{ carbon.dataSource }}</p>
        <p><strong>Last updated:</strong> {{ carbon.lastUpdated | date:'MMM yyyy' }}</p>
        <p class="verified-note">
          <span class="verified-dot"></span>
          Primary supplier data via SAP Sustainability Data Exchange
        </p>
      </div>
    </div>
  `
})
export class CarbonBadgeComponent implements OnInit {
  @Input() product!: Product & { carbonFootprintKgCO2e?: number; [key: string]: any };

  carbon: CarbonFootprintData | null = null;
  showMethodology = false;

  // 0.34 kgCO2e per km driven in an average EU petrol car (DEFRA 2024 factor)
  private readonly KG_CO2_PER_KM = 0.22;

  get drivingEquivalentKm(): number {
    return this.carbon ? Math.round(this.carbon.co2eKg / this.KG_CO2_PER_KM) : 0;
  }

  ngOnInit() {
    // Map OCC product response attributes → typed CarbonFootprintData
    if (this.product?.carbonFootprintKgCO2e != null) {
      this.carbon = {
        co2eKg:      this.product.carbonFootprintKgCO2e,
        scope1Kg:    this.product.carbonScope1KgCO2e ?? 0,
        dataSource:  this.product.carbonDataSource ?? 'SAP SFM',
        lastUpdated: this.product.carbonLastUpdated ?? '',
        isLowCarbon: this.product.carbonLowCarbonBadge ?? false,
        boundary:    this.product.carbonBoundary ?? 'Cradle-to-gate',
        pactVersion: this.product.carbonPactVersion ?? '2.1.0'
      };
    }
  }
}

The OCC API must be configured to expose the custom attributes. This is done in the Commerce Cloud product data mapper:

// occ-product-normalizer.module.ts
// Extend the Spartacus OCC normalizer to map custom carbon attributes

import { Injectable } from '@angular/core';
import { Converter, OccConfig } from '@spartacus/core';

// Tell the OCC layer which custom fields to request from the API
export const CARBON_OCC_PRODUCT_FIELDS =
  'carbonFootprintKgCO2e,' +
  'carbonScope1KgCO2e,' +
  'carbonDataSource,' +
  'carbonLastUpdated,' +
  'carbonLowCarbonBadge,' +
  'carbonBoundary,' +
  'carbonPactVersion';

// Merge into the Spartacus product fields configuration
export function provideCarbonProductFields(): OccConfig {
  return {
    backend: {
      occ: {
        endpoints: {
          product: {
            default: `products/\${productCode}?fields=DEFAULT,${CARBON_OCC_PRODUCT_FIELDS}`,
            details: `products/\${productCode}?fields=FULL,${CARBON_OCC_PRODUCT_FIELDS}`
          }
        }
      }
    }
  };
}

Layer 4 — Cart CO₂e Aggregation Service

The cart-level carbon summary panel (shown in the second mockup above) requires a service that aggregates CO₂e across all cart entries:

// cart-carbon.service.ts
// Aggregates per-product CO2e values across active cart entries

import { Injectable } from '@angular/core';
import { ActiveCartService } from '@spartacus/cart/base/core';
import { Observable, combineLatest } from 'rxjs';
import { map } from 'rxjs/operators';

export interface CartCarbonSummary {
  totalCO2eKg:         number;
  coveredItemCount:     number;
  totalItemCount:       number;
  drivingEquivalentKm:  number;
  offsetCostEur:        number;
  entries: Array<{
    productName: string;
    co2eKg:      number;
    quantity:    number;
    lineTotal:   number;
  }>;
}

@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })
export class CartCarbonService {

  // Offset cost factor: €0.045 per kgCO2e (ClimatePartner / EcoCart rate)
  private readonly OFFSET_COST_PER_KG_EUR = 0.045;
  private readonly KG_CO2_PER_KM          = 0.22;

  constructor(private activeCartService: ActiveCartService) {}

  getCartCarbonSummary(): Observable<CartCarbonSummary> {
    return this.activeCartService.getActive().pipe(
      map(cart => {
        const entries = cart.entries ?? [];
        let totalCO2e = 0;
        let covered   = 0;

        const lineItems = entries.map(entry => {
          const co2ePerUnit: number =
            (entry.product as any)?.carbonFootprintKgCO2e ?? 0;
          const qty      = entry.quantity ?? 1;
          const lineCO2e = co2ePerUnit * qty;

          if (co2ePerUnit > 0) { covered++; totalCO2e += lineCO2e; }

          return {
            productName: entry.product?.name ?? '',
            co2eKg:      lineCO2e,
            quantity:    qty,
            lineTotal:   (entry.totalPrice?.value ?? 0)
          };
        });

        return {
          totalCO2eKg:        Math.round(totalCO2e * 10) / 10,
          coveredItemCount:   covered,
          totalItemCount:     entries.length,
          drivingEquivalentKm: Math.round(totalCO2e / this.KG_CO2_PER_KM),
          offsetCostEur:      Math.round(totalCO2e * this.OFFSET_COST_PER_KG_EUR * 100) / 100,
          entries:            lineItems
        };
      })
    );
  }
}

Layer 3 — Real-Time Facade: BTP CAP Microservice

For Pattern B (real-time fetch at PDP load), a lightweight SAP CAP (Cloud Application Programming Model) service on BTP acts as the Carbon Data Facade:

// carbon-facade/srv/carbon-service.js
// SAP CAP service — Carbon Data Facade on BTP
// Proxies SFM PCF API with caching layer

const cds = require('@sap/cds');

module.exports = cds.service.impl(async function() {

  const SFM_BINDING = await cds.connect.to('SFM_PCF_API');

  // In-memory TTL cache (production: use Redis or SAP BTP Object Store)
  const cache   = new Map();
  const TTL_MS  = 4 * 60 * 60 * 1000; // 4-hour cache TTL

  this.on('READ', 'ProductFootprints', async (req) => {
    const { productId } = req.data;

    // Check cache first
    const cached = cache.get(productId);
    if (cached && Date.now() - cached.ts < TTL_MS) {
      return cached.data;
    }

    // Fetch from SFM Published Product Footprints API
    const result = await SFM_BINDING.run(
      SELECT.from('ProductFootprints')
        .where({ productId })
        .limit(1)
    );

    const footprint = result?.[0] ?? null;

    if (footprint) {
      // Transform PACT response → storefront-friendly shape
      const transformed = {
        productId,
        co2eKg:        parseFloat(footprint.pcf?.pCfExcludingBiogenic ?? '0'),
        scope1Kg:      parseFloat(footprint.pcf?.fossilGhgEmissions ?? '0'),
        boundary:      footprint.pcf?.boundaryProcessesDescription,
        pactVersion:   footprint.specVersion,
        lastUpdated:   footprint.reportingPeriodEnd,
        isLowCarbon:   parseFloat(footprint.pcf?.pCfExcludingBiogenic) < 8.0
      };
      cache.set(productId, { data: transformed, ts: Date.now() });
      return transformed;
    }

    return req.error(404, `No published footprint for product: ${productId}`);
  });
});

Key patterns

The PDP and cart mockups presented earlier in Section 6 illustrate four key patterns. Each has a distinct implementation path.

Pattern A — Carbon Badge on the PDP

Rendered by the CarbonBadgeComponent above. Key design decisions:

  • The percentile rank (e.g., "Top 18% in specific section") gives relative meaning to an absolute number most consumers cannot contextualise
  • The scope breakdown bar (Scope 1 / 2 / 3) is CSRD-aligned and educates consumers on what drives the footprint
  • The real-world equivalent ("equivalent to driving 28 km") is sourced from the DEFRA 2024 emission factor for a petrol car (0.22 kgCO₂e/km)
  • The methodology tooltip is the anti-greenwashing layer — a consumer who clicks it sees the exact data chain

Pattern B — Carbon Sort and Filter in Search

The ImpEx above adds carbonFootprintKgCO2e as a Solr-indexed, sortable field. The Spartacus search configuration to expose this in the facet panel:

// spartacus-configuration.module.ts
// Expose carbon sort option in the Composable Storefront search UI

import { provideConfig } from '@spartacus/core';
import { SearchboxConfig } from '@spartacus/storefront';

provideConfig({
  routing: {},
  i18n: {},
  // Extend the default product list component to surface carbon sort
  layoutConfig: {
    layoutSlots: {
      ProductListPageTemplate: {
        slots: ['ProductLeftRefinements', 'ProductListSlot']
      }
    }
  },
  // Register carbon sort options in the product list config
  view: {
    defaultPageSize: 12,
    infiniteScroll: { active: false }
  }
});

// In your product-list.module.ts, add to the sort options config:
export const CARBON_SORT_OPTIONS = [
  { code: 'relevance',    name: 'Relevance' },
  { code: 'topRated',     name: 'Top rated' },
  { code: 'price-asc',    name: 'Price: low to high' },
  { code: 'carbon-asc',   name: '🌱 Carbon: low to high' },  // ← new
  { code: 'carbon-desc',  name: 'Carbon: high to low' }
];

Pattern C — Cart Carbon Summary

The CartCarbonService above provides all data. The cart component subscribes and renders:

// cart-summary.component.ts (excerpt)
carbonSummary$: Observable<CartCarbonSummary>;

constructor(private cartCarbonService: CartCarbonService) {
  this.carbonSummary$ = this.cartCarbonService.getCartCarbonSummary();
}

// In template:
// <app-cart-carbon-panel [summary]="carbonSummary$ | async">
// </app-cart-carbon-panel>

Pattern D — My Sustainability Account Dashboard

A post-login dashboard aggregating a consumer's lifetime purchase carbon footprint. This requires a custom Commerce Cloud order history extension that sums the carbonFootprintKgCO2e values across historical order entries:

// order-history-carbon-aggregator.js
// SAP Commerce Cloud — Custom FlexibleSearch query
// Aggregates CO2e across all orders for a given customer

const query = `
  SELECT
    {oe:product},
    SUM({oe:quantity} * {p:carbonFootprintKgCO2e}) AS totalCO2eKg,
    COUNT(DISTINCT {o:pk}) AS orderCount
  FROM {OrderEntry AS oe
    JOIN Order AS o ON {oe:order} = {o:pk}
    JOIN Product AS p ON {oe:product} = {p:pk}
  }
  WHERE
    {o:user}              = ?userId
    AND {o:status}        = 'COMPLETE'
    AND {p:carbonFootprintKgCO2e} IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY {oe:product}
  ORDER BY totalCO2eKg DESC
`;

This powers a personalised view — "Your 2025 carbon footprint across purchases: 142 kgCO₂e — equivalent to flying London→Amsterdam and back" — the kind of narrative hook that drives account logins and return visits.

 

Conclusion

The opportunity is not simply to place a carbon number on a product page. It is to connect governed enterprise sustainability information with the digital buying journey in a way that preserves meaning, traceability, and customer trust.

SAP Commerce Cloud provides the extensible commerce foundation. SAP Sustainability Footprint Management provides the product-footprint context. SAP Green Ledger contributes the connection between carbon and financial dimensions, while SAP Sustainability Control Tower supports the wider sustainability-performance landscape. SAP Business Technology Platform provides the integration and extension layer that connects these responsibilities without moving calculation logic into the storefront.

Starting with a common product identifier, approved footprint data, and a transparent product-page experience creates a strong foundation. Search, cart, and account experiences can then be introduced where product coverage, comparability, governance, and customer value justify them.

The result is a commerce experience in which sustainability information is not merely stated. It is connected to governed enterprise data and presented with the context required for customers to understand it.

entry.title: An idea: ERP-native carbon accounting for Oil & Gas
entry.content:
## The GAP that keeps bothering me:

Here's what I find striking: SAP already holds some of the most granular production data in the industry. Volumes per well, flare rates per facility, throughput by day — it's all sitting in S/4 HANA upstream modules. Yet nobody has built the engine that turns that production data directly into carbon accounting. The production data and the carbon obligation live in two completely separate worlds and today companies bridge the gap with spreadsheets.

## The IDEA:

The idea I've been exploring is simple to state: *An ERP-native Carbon Accounting Engine. *

Instead of exporting production data and reconciling it in spreadsheets, the engine would read production records directly from S/4HANA — enriched with IoT/SCADA data where available — and calculate emissions in real time on SAP BTP, using a standard, auditable methodology. The output would be audit-ready from day one and shaped to whatever framework the jurisdiction needs: CSRD, IFRS S2, EU ETS, and so on.

No spreadsheets. No manual exports. No multi-month lag. The moment production data moves, the emissions number moves with it — and the calculation chain behind it is fully transparent for assurance.

## Why I think it matters:

Mandatory disclosure is expanding across jurisdictions, and investors are increasingly asking for facility-level, near-real-time data. What I find compelling is that "Every new regulation that gets passed doesn't break this idea — it just becomes another configuration of the same engine." That's why I believe building carbon accounting *inside* the ERP, rather than alongside it, is the defensible place to do it.

## Where I am with this:

To be clear: this is an idea at the concept stage. I've sketched out the architecture and put together a rough demo to sanity-check the flow, sharing the idea to get much sharper inputs and thought-process. 

A few questions I'd genuinely like your take on:

1. For you, is the bigger pain today the "data collection and reconciliation" or the "multi-framework reporting" on top of it?

2. Would a Scope 1- first wedge, anchored on the production data, be the right place to start — or would you anchor it somewhere else?

3. Is anyone on this forum already exploring adjacent territory? I'd be keen to connect and discuss further.

If you work in this space — sustainability, ENR— I'd really love to connect and share the thoughts with like-minded folks.

entry.title: WellToCredit: Why the ERP Should Be the System of Record for CCUS
entry.content:
WellToCredit: Why the ERP Should Be the System of Record for CCUS?

Last week, I wrote about a gap that bothers me: production data already inside S/4HANA could drive real-time Scope 1 disclosures — but instead, companies spend weeks reconciling spreadsheets to produce a number that's stale before it's signed off (An idea: ERP-native carbon accounting for Oil & Ga... - SAP Community).

Writing that post surfaced a question I couldn't leave alone ---- fine, so the ERP knows how much you emit. Then what?

The number is only half the story

When an Upstream operator calculates its Scope 1 emissions — venting, fugitive leaks, flaring, combustion exhaust — it produces a liability. A disclosure obligation.

What almost no one has built is a system that treats that same number as the starting point for a value chain.

The CO₂ that vents from a wellhead is a physical gas, at a location you operate, in volumes you can measure. Capture it, compress it and two things become possible:

Inject it into a depleting reservoir — and you recover more oil through enhanced recovery. Wells past their primary peak get a productive second life leading to increased revenue.

Store it permanently in deep geological formations — This is the interesting path. Inject that captured CO₂ into deep geological formations — depleted reservoirs, saline aquifers, sealed by cap rock that has contained fluids for millions of years — and something changes fundamentally. The subsurface becomes a carbon vault. Not a temporary offset purchased from a project on another continent. A verified, permanently sequestered volume, stored in geology you operate, traceable from the emission event to the injection well to the formation itself. That is exactly the kind of carbon credit that institutional buyers and regulators are now demanding — and almost no operator can produce one today, because the data chain that would prove it doesn't exist inside a single system.

That distinction matters. A credit backed by verified tonnes stored a kilometre underground is categorically more valuable than one purchased from a forestry project elsewhere. Markets are moving fast in that direction.

Why now?

The economics shifted faster than most operators expected. Carbon storage now carries a real price — the US tax credit for verified geological sequestration has moved from marginal incentive to material project driver. At the same time, carbon intensity is becoming a trade cost in major import markets, meaning high-intensity upstream production will soon carry a real border surcharge — and system-generated sequestration records, not manual reports, are what will differentiate. Meanwhile, the world's largest energy companies need credits that survive third-party assurance, which means a documented chain of custody from emission source through injection to ongoing subsurface monitoring. Permanence is becoming the new standard, and the industry isn't ready for it.

The IDEA: WellToCredit

I'm calling this WellToCredit — the arc from wellhead emission, through capture, through permanent geological sequestration, to a verified carbon credit on the balance sheet.

The data this requires — emission sources, capture equipment, CO₂ transport, injection operations, subsurface MRV(monitoring, reporting and verification) monitoring, compliance submissions, credit accounting — already flows through SAP in some form in most Upstream operations. Building this alongside the ERP and reconciling two systems indefinitely is the path the industry already regrets taking with carbon accounting.

I think the system of record for the full CCUS chain should be the ERP. This is a concept I'm developing — no demo yet, but the business case is one I believe holds.

Three questions I'd genuinely welcome challenge on

  1. At what scale does the sequestration credit value actually cover site characterisation costs — and has anyone done that analysis for a real basin?
  2. Where does subsurface MRV monitoring data live today, and has anyone successfully connected it to a compliance or financial system?
  3. Is anyone in this community already working on the data architecture behind CCUS in SAP? I'd rather compare notes than work in parallel.
